title: The Painting Survived a Breakup, a World War, and a Decade Behind a Wall
standfirst: In 1911 Kandinsky borrowed a craft he'd picked up from Bavarian farmhouses to paint the Book of Revelation on the back of a pane of glass. In 1914 he left it behind in Munich and never set foot in Germany again. It survives today only because the woman who kept it hid it from the Nazis instead of handing it back.

sections.heading: The Technique Belonged to Farmhouses Long Before It Belonged to Him
sections.body:
Gabriele Münter [bought a house](https://www.dasblaueland.de/en/poi/muenter-haus) in the Bavarian market town of Murnau on 21 August 1909, on the shore of the Staffelsee, and for the next five summers she and Kandinsky lived among people who still painted saints and votive scenes on the back of a pane of glass — a rural craft with no academy, no signature, and no place in a Munich gallery. They collected examples and started making their own.

This panel is one result. The Lenbachhaus catalogs it as ink, oil, and [gold and silver bronze](https://www.lenbachhaus.de/digital/sammlung-online/detail/allerheiligen-i-30013561) worked onto the reverse of a small sheet of glass, thirty-four by forty centimetres, set into a frame Kandinsky painted himself. He made it in 1911, and he used the farmhouse technique for a subject no local sign-painter had ever needed it for: the end of the world, straight out of the Book of Revelation.

sections.heading: The Museum That Owns It Still Hedges on Who Some of the Saints Are
sections.body:
The Lenbachhaus's [own catalog entry](https://www.lenbachhaus.de/digital/sammlung-online/detail/allerheiligen-i-30013561) can't fully identify its own cast. Beneath a trumpeting angel, it lists Saint George on a white horse, Saint Vladimir, and a female saint holding a candle — then hedges on two more figures, suggesting they might be the martyred Russian princes Boris and Gleb, or just as plausibly the Bavarian saints Cosmas and Damian. Three mourners and a prone monk fill out the crowd. The panel is built as an argument with itself: a walled city under a red sun on one side, a dark moon and a crucifix on the other.

Kandinsky returned to the same cast that same year in oil, twice. [One of the results](https://www.lenbachhaus.de/digital/sammlung-online/detail/allerheiligen-ii-30018461), Allerheiligen II, is catalogued as a close relative of the glass panel that renders the same figures — plus the prophet Elijah ascending in a fiery chariot and the evangelist John staring up at the angel — in a far more legible form. If there is a study and a finished statement here, the glass version, by the museum's own account, might be the study.

sections.heading: That Same Year, He Argued This Kind of Craft Was Art on Equal Terms
sections.body:
In 1911 the jury of Kandinsky's own Munich art association rejected one of his increasingly abstract canvases. He and Franz Marc resigned and mounted a rival show that December under a new name, Der Blaue Reiter. The almanac the two of them edited the following year put more than a hundred and forty reproductions on equal footing: [folk art and children's drawings](https://www.theartstory.org/movement/der-blaue-reiter/) sat next to paintings by trained masters, with no ranking between them.

The point being made was that training and polish were beside the point next to what a picture expressed. A pane of glass painted by a farmhouse craftsman for a hallway, and a canvas hung in a Munich gallery, were on that logic doing the same job. Kandinsky had already tested the argument on himself. He had taken the farmhouse technique and used it to paint the Apocalypse.

sections.heading: In 1914 He Left the Painting in Munich and Never Went Back
sections.body:
When war broke out in August 1914, Kandinsky and [Gabriele Münter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabriele_M%C3%BCnter) fled together to Switzerland, then lived apart for most of the war. By 1916 Kandinsky, back in Russia, had begun a relationship with a seventeen-year-old, Nina Andreevskaya; they married in 1917. Münter did not learn of the marriage until 1920. The two never met again.

What happened to the paintings Kandinsky left behind is told differently depending on whose account you read. [One version](https://www.theartstory.org/artist/munter-gabriele/) has Münter spending the 1920s trying to recover work still in Kandinsky's own hands, seeking what one scholar calls moral amends rather than money. [Another account](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabriele_M%C3%BCnter) has her returning some paintings and drawings to him while keeping others in storage. What both agree on is the outcome: a large body of work Kandinsky and Münter had made together in Munich and Murnau, this glass panel among it, stayed in Bavaria with her, and never went back to him.

sections.heading: It Survived Behind a Wall Because She Never Handed It Over
sections.body:
None of that made the painting safe. Kandinsky was one of the artists targeted when the Nazi regime seized [more than five thousand works](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Degenerate_Art_exhibition) from German museums in 1937; six hundred and fifty of them went on display, hung crookedly and mocked with slogans, in Munich's Degenerate Art exhibition that July, and nearly five thousand were burned in Berlin on 20 March 1939.

Münter had no museum's protection, and every reason to expect a search. She hid her holdings of Kandinsky and the rest of the Blue Rider circle in the [basement of her Murnau house](https://www.lenbachhaus.de/en/museum/foundations/gabriele-muenter-and-johannes-eichner-foundation). The house was searched more than once. Nothing was found. In 1952 she let Hans Konrad Roethel, who would later run the Lenbachhaus itself, in to see what she had kept hidden. Five years after that, for her eightieth birthday, she gave most of the collection away — well over eighty oil paintings and hundreds of drawings, this small glass panel included. It is catalogued today as GMS 107, in the museum her own hiding place eventually filled.
